content: A nursing school is an educational institution, or a part of one, that provides the necessary education and training to become a fully qualified nurse. The structure and requirements of nursing education and qualifications differ significantly across the globe. Florence Nightingale was a pioneer in establishing nursing schools. In 1860, she founded the Nightingale Training School for Nurses at St. Thomas' Hospital in London. Her primary goal was to train nurses to a professional standard, focusing on developing observation skills and sensitivity to patient needs. These trained nurses were then prepared to work in hospitals across the United Kingdom and internationally. Her influence led to the integration of nursing as a formal course in many British universities. The University of Manchester was among the first institutions in England to offer nursing as a degree-level course. Entry requirements for nursing programs in the UK typically include five Standard Grades/GCSEs, including English, mathematics, and a science subject (preferably biology), along with two Highers/A-Levels. Mature students over the age of 21 can also enter through college access courses or relevant work experience, such as roles as health or nursing assistants. Nursing education in the UK is a three-year program that combines classroom coursework with practical placements in healthcare settings. The first year focuses on foundational knowledge, including anatomy, physiology, and basic healthcare. In the second year, students specialize in one of four branches: adult nursing, pediatric nursing, mental health nursing, or learning disability nursing. Placements are tailored to the chosen specialty, allowing students to gain essential skills in their specific field. The third year concludes the program, with students having the option to complete degree-level essays or graduate with a diploma. Midwifery students follow a distinct pathway, specializing from the first year. Upon graduation, newly qualified nurses must register with the Nursing and Midwifery Council to legally practice and apply for jobs. In the United States, the Yale School of Nursing became the first autonomous nursing school in 1923, with its own dean, faculty, budget, and degree standards aligned with the university. Its curriculum was based on an educational plan rather than hospital service needs. In 1956, Columbia University School of Nursing became the first in the U.S. to offer a master's degree in a clinical nursing specialty. Prerequisites for nursing programs often include courses in mathematics, English, and basic sciences, with additional requirements in biology, anatomy, and physiology. Core coursework includes anatomy, physiology, pathology, and pharmacology, with a strong emphasis on procedural skills such as intravenous and urinary catheter insertion, sterile dressing changes, medication administration, and physical examinations. After acquiring basic skills in the first semester, students rotate through various units, including obstetrics, mental health, medical-surgical, oncology, critical care, and pediatrics, to gain a comprehensive understanding of nursing. Many nursing students and schools utilize medical and healthcare educational software as a training aid. Graduates of U.S. nursing programs are qualified to take the national licensing exam for Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) or Registered Nurses (RNs). Degrees granted in nursing include the Diploma in Nursing, Associate of Science in Nursing, Bachelor of Science in Nursing, Master of Science in Nursing, and Doctor of Nursing Science. After completing a nursing program (Diploma, Associate, or Bachelor's), graduates are required to pass the National Council Licensure Exam (NCLEX-RN) to practice as registered nurses. Historically, attending nursing school required proximity to a physical institution or relocation. However, the advent of online nursing programs has expanded opportunities for prospective students. These innovative programs allow students to take classes remotely, creating a nationwide community of learners. This format enables busy adults to pursue formal academic degrees without leaving their jobs, families, or communities to attend on-campus classes.
